messages.subject_clean: [JIRA] (SPARKR-89) Memoize frequently queried vals in RDD, such as numPartitions, count etc.
messages.body_plain:
Shivaram Venkataraman <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=shivaram> commented on  SPARKR-89 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-89>

Re: Memoize frequently queried vals in RDD, such as numPartitions, count etc. <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-89>

One thing I've noticed is that while using SparkR in RStudio, the `count` function seems to be called frequently by the IDE – I think this is to show some stats about variables in the workspace etc. but this is not great in SparkR as we trigger a job every time count is called.

Memoization would help in this case, but we should also see if there is some better way to interact with RStudio.

Re: Function dependencies are captured too late, so that the value of free variables have already changed <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-142>

It is fixed by https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg/pull/186, and no need for extra changes. I save the closure with each function and use nested functions in the pipeline as before.

However, if you could remember, an alternative way is using a accumulator to store functions. One of the benefits of that might be that we could support "..." in lapply, by storing the ... argument in each element of the accumulator. That would be a nice feature, but a minor issue.

When submitting a job with sparkR-submit

/usr/lib64/R/library/SparkR/sparkR-submit --master yarn-client examples/pi.R yarn-client 4

The first cut of the Column API was merged in https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg/pull/188

Some other APIs which would be good to support include

Column selection:

  # Selecting the first column
  df[[1]]
  df[["V1"]]
  df[,1]

  # Selecting the first two columns
  df[,1:2]
  df[,c("V1", "V2")]

   # Column assignment, mutating the DF
   df$V3 <- df$V1 + df$V2

I think we can implement this by overriding the `[`, `[[` and assignment operators in the DataFrame S4 class (http://stackoverflow.com/questions/24253048/whats-the-difference-between-setmethod-and-set-setreplacemethod might be useful)

Re: Remote Dependencies Documentation <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-218>

SparkR uses SBT/Maven to build the necessary Java dependencies. Unfortunately its not very easy to use maven in a offline setting (some threads like [1] may be useful) but there are couple of workarounds that you could use
You could ask Maven to make its connections go through a proxy server if you have a setup that allows for that [2]
Or you could clone the SparkR repository on any machine which has internet access, build a self-contained binary package as a tar.gz and distribute that to your servers. To do that you can run something like

cd SparkR-pkg
R CMD INSTALL --build pkg

and this should produce a file named SparkR_0.1.tgz – The only things you need to ensure is that you build this on a machine with the same architecture and R version as the target server

[1] http://stackoverflow.com/questions/7233328/how-do-i-configure-maven-for-offline-development
[2] http://maven.apache.org/guides/mini/guide-proxies.html

If we have a sparkR.stop() in any unit test, then the later tests will fail as:

collect on 44 failed with java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Object not found 44
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Object not found 44
	at edu.berkeley.cs.amplab.sparkr.SparkRBackendHandler.handleMethodCall(SparkRBackendHandler.scala:91)
	at edu.berkeley.cs.amplab.sparkr.SparkRBackendHandler.channelRead0(SparkRBackendHandler.scala:60)
	at edu.berkeley.cs.amplab.sparkr.SparkRBackendHandler.channelRead0(SparkRBackendHandler.scala:22)
	at io.netty.channel.SimpleChannelInboundHandler.channelRead(SimpleChannelInboundHandler.java:105)
	at io.netty.channel.AbstractChannelHandlerContext.invokeChannelRead(AbstractChannelHandlerContext.java:333)
	at io.netty.channel.AbstractChannelHandlerContext.fireChannelRead(AbstractChannelHandlerContext.java:319)
	at io.netty.handler.codec.MessageToMessageDecoder.channelRead(MessageToMessageDecoder.java:103)
	at io.netty.channel.AbstractChannelHandlerContext.invokeChannelRead(AbstractChannelHandlerContext.java:333)
	at io.netty.channel.AbstractChannelHandlerContext.fireChannelRead(AbstractChannelHandlerContext.java:319)
	at io.netty.handler.codec.ByteToMessageDecoder.channelRead(ByteToMessageDecoder.java:163)
	at io.netty.channel.AbstractChannelHandlerContext.invokeChannelRead(AbstractChannelHandlerContext.java:333)
	at io.netty.channel.AbstractChannelHandlerContext.fireChannelRead(AbstractChannelHandlerContext.java:319)
	at io.netty.channel.DefaultChannelPipeline.fireChannelRead(DefaultChannelPipeline.java:787)
	at io.netty.channel.nio.AbstractNioByteChannel$NioByteUnsafe.read(AbstractNioByteChannel.java:130)
	at io.netty.channel.nio.NioEventLoop.processSelectedKey(NioEventLoop.java:511)
	at io.netty.channel.nio.NioEventLoop.processSelectedKeysOptimized(NioEventLoop.java:468)
	at io.netty.channel.nio.NioEventLoop.processSelectedKeys(NioEventLoop.java:382)
	at io.netty.channel.nio.NioEventLoop.run(NioEventLoop.java:354)
	at io.netty.util.concurrent.SingleThreadEventExecutor$2.run(SingleThreadEventExecutor.java:116)
	at io.netty.util.concurrent.DefaultThreadFactory$DefaultRunnableDecorator.run(DefaultThreadFactory.java:137)
	at java.lang.Thread.run(Thread.java:745)

The reason is that we track all the reference of Java objects in two global environments. All new SparkContext will count the Java objects from 0, they could be confusing, for example, the reference for Java object in previous JVM, will remove the Java object with same ID in current JVM, then you will fail to access this Java object.

S4 methods are defined with function setGeneric and setMethod. Conventionally, all setGeneric declarations could be moved into a single file in cases that there are multiple setMethod definitions in different file (for different signatures). There could be a file called "00-generics.R" to have all the setGenerics. messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've built SparkR to run on my AWS EC2 cluster under CDH 5.3.1 through Yarn. I've successfully run a number of Spark jobs but it always seems to only use 2 executors running on 2 of my 5 nodes. Can anyone tell me how to set the number of executors to use in Cloudera Manager? Do you have to use spark-submit to do this? Also, am I correct in thinking that the optimal number of executors to use is one per node?

Cheers,

Sean

messages.subject: Re: How to set number of executors when running SparkR on CDH 5.3.1 cluster
messages.subject_clean: How to set number of executors when running SparkR on CDH 5.3.1 cluster
messages.body_plain:
You can try using the new `sparkR-submit` scripts [1] to run things on YARN. These scripts should take the same arguments as spark-submit, so you can pass YARN specific configuration like total number of executors to request. The page on 'Running Spark on YARN' has some useful examples [2].

And to answer your second question, for most cases its good to have one executor per machine and configure that executor to use all the cores on the machine.

Thanks
Shivaram

[1] https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg#running-on-a-cluster-using-sparkr-submit
[2] http://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/running-on-yarn.html

messages.subject: SparkR branch updates, merge plans
messages.subject_clean: SparkR branch updates, merge plans
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

As some of you might be aware we recently submitted a proposal to merge SparkR with the mainline Apache Spark project [1]. Given the developments around new DataFrame APIs and the stabilization of other components like the RDD API, spark-submit and JVM backend, I think this is a good time to create a pull request for the merge.

The merge process will cause some changes to our development workflow and I have detailed a plan for that below. I plan to start this in a week or so after merging the PRs that are currently open. Do let me know if you have any feedback or questions.

Thanks
Shivaram

SparkR Merge Steps

1.  Our development right now happens on two branches `master` and `sparkr-sql`. The latter is used for developing the DataFrame API which ships with Spark 1.3. To support existing users, the convention we will use is that the master branch will support Spark versions 0.9 to 1.2. We will rename the `sparkr-sql` branch to `branch-1.3` and this will support Spark 1.3.
After the merge we will release SparkR as a part of Spark 1.4

2. The master branch and `sparkr-sql` branch have diverged a bit and we will port relevant changes to make them share a common baseline. The only changes in `sparkr-sql` that will not be in `master` will be those related to DataFrames. We will also merge all the PRs currently open on the SparkR repository before starting a code move.

3. We will create a new repository at https://github.com/amplab-extras/spark as a fork of the Apache Spark repository. This repository will be used to stage our merge PR and we will continue development on this repository for any bug fixes, documentation changes etc.

4. After the merge, development will continue on the Apache Spark repository. We will add a SparkR developers guide to the Spark contributors wiki.

5. We will also transition the JIRA issues and related documentation to the Spark repository after the code merge. I will post another message before we do that.

[1] https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-5654

messages.body_plain:
People's github cred won't go disappear on the current SparkR repo, but you are right that they won't be inherited into Spark. Only new work people do will show up in Spark's history. It's definitely one downside of this approach, but with Spark SQL it didn't seem to matter much, since most of the same people just continued contributing to it as part of the upstream project.

Overall, my advice is for SparkR to focus on making sure it can be merged in a way that minimizes the impact to the existing Spark project. This is the best way to make sure everyone is enthusiastic about the merge. Unfortunately, a naive "git merge" would pollute the git history in a way that has adverse consequences for many people in the Spark ecosystem, even those who do not use or intend to use SparkR.

- Patrick

Hi Sailesh

The DataFrame API for SparkR is being developed in the sparkr-sql branch of the github repo (https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg/tree/sparkr-sql). We don't yet have a user guide for this but the examples in the roxygen docs and the test cases (https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg/blob/sparkr-sql/pkg/inst/tests/test_sparkSQL.R) should give you a pointer on how to get started

Note that the DataFrame API is a work in progress, so we'd appreciate any feedback you have.

Thanks
Shivaram

> logs = context.load("s3n://path/to/data.json", "json")
>
> but R console is unable to recognize. I tried replacing context with SC but also didn't work
>

>
>
>
> Regards

Replace dot with underscore in column names <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-233>
Issue Type:    Sub-task
Assignee:   Davies <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=davies>
Created:   16/Mar/15 10:30 AM
Priority:    Major
Reporter:   Shivaram Venkataraman <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=shivaram>

SparkSQL does not support having dots in column names (see https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-2775) . When we convert a local R data frame to
Spark DataFrame we should replace dot with underscores. We could also print a warning message about this

To reproduce the problem try something like

df <- createDataFrame(sqlCtx, iris) # iris has columns Sepal.Width, Petal.Width etc.
df$Petal.Width # Throws an error

messages.body_plain:
Shivaram Venkataraman <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=shivaram> created an issue

SparkR <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR> /  <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-234> SPARKR-234 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-234>
Improve performance for parallelize <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-234>
Issue Type:    Improvement
Assignee:   Unassigned
Created:   16/Mar/15 8:37 PM
Priority:    Minor
Reporter:   Shivaram Venkataraman <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=shivaram>

The parallelize operation in SparkR creates a ParallelCollectionRDD which ships part of the collection in its partition information. This creates large tasks which throw a warning and slow down execution. Instead we could follow a trick similar to PySpark where we create a local file and then call `objectFile` on the local file to create the RDD.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul

So it looks like the maven command was successful but the install failed after that when I tried to run a windows command using `cmd`.

Couple of things that might help debug this:

1. Are you running this from Powershell or the terminal launched with `cmd`?
2. In either case could you see if running just `cmd` in your terminal has any effect ? If you still get the `cmd not found` error it means that your PATH variable is somehow not correct (might have a typo while you were editing it for maven or Java etc.)

Thanks
Shivaram

messages.body_plain:
Hi all

A quick update on the merge plan that I outlined last week. We have now created a Spark fork at https://github.com/amplab-extras/spark and I'd like to particularly thank Davies for his help in porting our code (with history [1]) over to the new repository.

There are still a couple of PRs open on the old repository [2] that I'd like to include before making an official merge PR to Apache Spark, but in the meanwhile I'll be asking developers to send a version of their PRs to this repository as well.

We have an updated README for building, running SparkR at https://github.com/amplab-extras/spark/blob/R/R/README.md and this might be especially useful for those who are new to Spark development.

Please let me know if you have any questions / clarifications

Thanks
Shivaram

[1] For example see the per-line history in RDD.R at https://github.com/amplab-extras/spark/blame/R/R/pkg/R/RDD.R

[2] https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg/pulls

messages.body_plain:
Davies <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=davies> commented on  SPARKR-234 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-234>

Re: Improve performance for parallelize <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-234>

The reason we use local file to pass the data into JVM is that Py4j has very pool performance with large data (because of text protocol). After that, we still use parallelize() in JVM.

The local file can not be accessed by other workers in cluster, so we can not avoid the ParallelCollectionRDD without a distributed file system.

Developing package that imports SparkR. There is a function in that package that calls lapplyPartition with a function argument that uses in its body some functions private to the package. When run, the computation fails because R can not find the private function (details below). If I fully qualify them with otherpackage:::private.function, the error moves down to the next private function. This used to work some time ago, I've been working on other stuff for a little while. This should also work by regular R scope rules. I apologize I don't have a minimal test case ready, but this was discovered developing plyrmr and the list of dependencies is long enough that it's a little bit of a burden to make you install it. I think I can put together a toy package to demonstrate the problem, if that helps.

messages.subject: Building a Random Forest model with SparkR
messages.subject_clean: Building a Random Forest model with SparkR
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've been working on building a Random Forest model on my modest AWS cluster (6 nodes each with 16 cores and 32G RAM) using Spark. My training set is pretty big (~30,000 rows and ~2,000 columns) so won't run on a single node. I had cobbled together some code to build the model as a Map Reduce job, and now I've hacked some code together to do this in Spark (see below). It takes about 15 sec to build a model on my cluster using this code (an equivalent implementation as a MapReduce job took about 15 mins).

In this example my training set data is located in HDFS as a csv file with no column or row names. The column names of the training set are instead saved in the file train.names.rda which is loaded in before building the model. To combine the random forests together into a single model at the end, I use the my_combine function that was helpfully provided by Joran at http://stackoverflow.com/questions/19170130/combining-random-forests-built-with-different-training-sets-in-r.

I'm sure there is likely to be a better way of doing it than this, so please feel free to suggest improvements (or alternative approaches)!

### START

# Load libraries
library(randomForest)
library(SparkR)

# Set spark memory allocation (important even though I set the spark executor and driver memories when initializing the Spark context, as without it I run into Java heap space errors)
Sys.setenv(SPARK_MEM="40g")

# Initialise Spark context
sc <- sparkR.init(master="yarn-client",sparkEnvir=list(spark.executor.memory="24g",spark.driver.memory="24g",spark.executor.instances="5",spark.executor.cores="16", spark.driver.maxResultSize="10g"))

# Pass randomForest package to all nodes
includePackage(sc,randomForest)

### Build randomForest models of 10 trees each for entire data set sliced into 50 chunks (so 500 trees in the forest)

# Load the column names of the training set
load("train.names.rda")

# Define RDD with 50 slices
rdd <- textFile(sc, "hdfs:<server_address>/user/spark/spark_training.csv",50)

# Define mapPartition function to build randomForest models
rf <- mapPartitions(rdd, function(input) {

# Parse the RDD into a data frame
df <- data.frame(do.call('rbind',strsplit(as.character(input),',',fixed=TRUE)))

# Set the data frame column names
names(df) <- train.names

# Fix the data type to numeric for all but the classification column
for (i in 1:(ncol(df)-1)){
df[,i] <- as.numeric(as.character(df[,i]))
}

# Get rid of quotation marks in classification column
df$MyClass <- as.factor(gsub("\"","", df$MyClass))
# Build the RF model
randomForest(df[,-ncol(df)],df[,ncol(df)],ntree=10)
})

# Build the models
output.rf<- collect(rf)

# Define function to split output list into individual models and combine into one uber model
uberRF <- function (x) {
        j=1
        rf.list <- list()
        for (i in 1:(length(x)/18)){
                temp <-x[j:(i*18)]
                class(temp) <- "randomForest"
                varname <- paste("rf",i,sep="")
                assign(varname,temp)
                j = j + 18
                rf.list[[length(rf.list)+1]] <- temp
        }

        # Combine the models together
        final.rf <- do.call(my_combine, rf.list)
        final.rf
}

# Combine the RF models
forest <- uberRF(output.rf)

### END

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

It was great to see SparkR treated as first class citizen during Spark Summit East talks.
I wanted to check if there is any plans of supporting Spark's streaming with R? I see there is jira ticket open with no updates.

My requirement is to use a model developed in R on a stream of incoming input. I don't really need to have streaming context accessed in R. Its more like a Storm Bolt written in R.
I want to avoid starting R process for each block. Do you have any thoughts on having a "R process" per worker that can take input, apply a function and return output? Something like Rserve may be??

Thanks,
Srikanth

messages.subject: Re: Building a Random Forest model with SparkR
messages.subject_clean: Building a Random Forest model with SparkR
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean

Great to know that your random forest implementation is faster now. I am not much of an expert on random forests, but I asked some other machine learning experts in the AMPLab about this:

1. There is a distributed random forests implementation in Spark's MLLib. Unfortunately we don't have R bindings for this yet, but Dan Putler has been working on this and we should have this soon.

2. For the native R version, one thing that might improve the statistical properties is if each partition was sampled with replacement from the original dataset instead of having it partitioned. This is similar to creating bootstrap samples on the original data. However its tricky to create these sample directly using RDDs. BTW can your data be loaded in the memory of a single machine ? If that is the case you can try to create 'N' partitions by doing sampling with replacement on a single machine and then call parallelize on the 'N' partitions. However I don't know if this overhead will be worth the improvements in accuracy.

Thanks
Shivaram

On Thu, Mar 19, 2015 at 5:15 PM, Sean Farrell <drsaf...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi all,
>
> I've been working on building a Random Forest model on my modest AWS cluster (6 nodes each with 16 cores and 32G RAM) using Spark. My training set is pretty big (~30,000 rows and ~2,000 columns) so won't run on a single node. I had cobbled together some code to build the model as a Map Reduce job, and now I've hacked some code together to do this in Spark (see below). It takes about 15 sec to build a model on my cluster using this code (an equivalent implementation as a MapReduce job took about 15 mins).
>
> In this example my training set data is located in HDFS as a csv file with no column or row names. The column names of the training set are instead saved in the file train.names.rda which is loaded in before building the model. To combine the random forests together into a single model at the end, I use the my_combine function that was helpfully provided by Joran at http://stackoverflow.com/questions/19170130/combining-random-forests-built-with-different-training-sets-in-r.
>
> I'm sure there is likely to be a better way of doing it than this, so please feel free to suggest improvements (or alternative approaches)!
>
>
> ### START
>
> # Load libraries
> library(randomForest)
> library(SparkR)
>
> # Set spark memory allocation (important even though I set the spark executor and driver memories when initializing the Spark context, as without it I run into Java heap space errors)
> Sys.setenv(SPARK_MEM="40g")
>
> # Initialise Spark context
> sc <- sparkR.init(master="yarn-client",sparkEnvir=list(spark.executor.memory="24g",spark.driver.memory="24g",spark.executor.instances="5",spark.executor.cores="16", spark.driver.maxResultSize="10g"))
>
> # Pass randomForest package to all nodes
> includePackage(sc,randomForest)
>
>
> ### Build randomForest models of 10 trees each for entire data set sliced into 50 chunks (so 500 trees in the forest)
>
> # Load the column names of the training set
> load("train.names.rda")
>
> # Define RDD with 50 slices
> rdd <- textFile(sc, "hdfs:<server_address>/user/spark/spark_training.csv",50)
>
> # Define mapPartition function to build randomForest models
> rf <- mapPartitions(rdd, function(input) {
>
> # Parse the RDD into a data frame
> df <- data.frame(do.call('rbind',strsplit(as.character(input),',',fixed=TRUE)))
>
> # Set the data frame column names
> names(df) <- train.names
>
> # Fix the data type to numeric for all but the classification column
> for (i in 1:(ncol(df)-1)){
> df[,i] <- as.numeric(as.character(df[,i]))
> }
>
> # Get rid of quotation marks in classification column
> df$MyClass <- as.factor(gsub("\"","", df$MyClass))
> # Build the RF model
> randomForest(df[,-ncol(df)],df[,ncol(df)],ntree=10)
> })
>
> # Build the models
> output.rf<- collect(rf)
>
> # Define function to split output list into individual models and combine into one uber model
> uberRF <- function (x) {
>         j=1
>         rf.list <- list()
>         for (i in 1:(length(x)/18)){
>                 temp <-x[j:(i*18)]
>                 class(temp) <- "randomForest"
>                 varname <- paste("rf",i,sep="")
>                 assign(varname,temp)
>                 j = j + 18
>                 rf.list[[length(rf.list)+1]] <- temp
>         }
>
>         # Combine the models together
>         final.rf <- do.call(my_combine, rf.list)
>         final.rf
> }
>
> # Combine the RF models
> forest <- uberRF(output.rf)
>
> ### END

> --

messages.subject: Re: SparkR Streaming
messages.subject_clean: SparkR Streaming
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Shivaram for the clarification. I somehow thought that in SparkR the Scala worker was internally launching a new R process during each stage. Did that change recently or was that the behavior from beginning?

Davies,
Thanks for listing out priority for SparkR. That really helps(although I'd have loved to see streaming up the list!!)
I'm not sure if forking R process would take just a few ms. Counting the time it would take to fork, setup environment, source one or two R files and load couple of libraries.

Thanks,
Srikanth

On Fri, Mar 20, 2015 at 3:08 PM, Davies Liu <dav...@databricks.com> wrote:
> I think SparkR is still in early stage, we are focus on API for Spark
> Core and SQL, which should
> be most important ones for data scientists. MLlib may come before streaming.
>
> The model in Spark Streaming is much different than Storm, microbatch
> VS pipeline. The overhead of schedule a batch in Spark Stream is about
> 100ms, which is much higher than Storm, then forking a R process for
> each batch is acceptable (which contribute a few of ms).
>
> We re-use the workers in PySpark, the most benefits is that we could
> re-used the broadcasted objects, but the implementation is
> complicated, introduced several bugs. We should avoid that in SparkR
> (at least in near future).

>
>
> On Fri, Mar 20, 2015 at 10:53 AM, Shivaram Venkataraman
> <shivaram.v...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > I'm not an expert in Spark streaming and Davies (cc'd) can probably throw
> > some light on how one can use something like a Storm Bolt in Spark
> > streaming.
> >
> > Regarding the second point of starting R processes each time, we already use
> > a long running R daemon on each machine and because of that the fork
> > overhead should be pretty low for each worker. We also have PR open to add
> > profiling for this [1], so we can measure how much overhead we have.
> >
> > Thanks
> > Shivaram
> >
> > [1] https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg/pull/208
> >
> > On Thu, Mar 19, 2015 at 5:39 PM, Srikanth <srika...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> Hi all,
> >>
> >> It was great to see SparkR treated as first class citizen during Spark
> >> Summit East talks.
> >> I wanted to check if there is any plans of supporting Spark's streaming
> >> with R? I see there is jira ticket open with no updates.
> >>
> >> My requirement is to use a model developed in R on a stream of incoming
> >> input. I don't really need to have streaming context accessed in R. Its more
> >> like a Storm Bolt written in R.
> >> I want to avoid starting R process for each block. Do you have any
> >> thoughts on having a "R process" per worker that can take input, apply a
> >> function and return output? Something like Rserve may be??
> >>
> >> Thanks,
> >> Srikanth

Antonio Piccolboni <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=piccolbo> commented on  SPARKR-237 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-237>

Re: private package functions unavailable when using lapplyPartition in package <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-237>

I would like to summarize the discussion that went on in a pull request https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/plyrmr/pull/72 to unify the subject under this ticket.
What it appears is that this problem depends of replacing getDependencies with cleanClosure and that it is unfixable in the short term. @hao proposed workarounds for dependent packages that include: fully qualifying all function calls; rename some variables according to unstated rules; modifying enclosing environment for promises in a way that is neither backward compatible nor consistent with R semantics (promises are not limited to one enclosing environment equal to GlobalEnv). These are extremely heavy handed, breaking the package in other ways and would be impossible to hide from the end user as the API accepts user defined functions and expressions in several if not most calls. So I am not trying to be difficult, but we can't adopt the workarounds. Considering that SparkR-238 is still open and probably related, my suggestion would be to revert to getDependencies for the moment being and make changes incrementally from there. @hao says getDependencies had correctness issues as well but I would like some detail about it, as plyrmr tests as well SparkR's own passed before cleanClosure was merged.

Considering that SparkR-238 is still open and probably related, my suggestion would be to revert to getDependencies for the moment being and make changes incrementally from there. @hao says getDependencies had correctness issues as well but I would like some detail about it, as plyrmr tests as well SparkR's own passed before cleanClosure was merged.

(+sparkr-dev@)

Hi Wu,

Based on the info I think you could do something along the following lines:

1) Use `take(rdd, 1)` to obtain the target point assuming 1st element in your RDD is the target.  With this, the SparkR driver node will have the two coordinates.

2) Then you could do `lapply(rdd, func)` where in func you calculate this distance between each element and the target, making use of the above coordinates directly.  (This works because closure serialization will capture the two numbers made available in the driver, and ship them to SparkR workers.)  This call returns a new RDD storing the desired distances.

If you want to learn more about Spark's programming model in general, take a look at [1].

Zongheng

[1] http://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/quick-start.html

Created:   31/Mar/15 2:06 PM
Priority:    Major
Reporter:   hao <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=hlin>

When I try run LR example by
./sparkR examples/logistic_regression.R local[2] /home/ubuntu/workspace/spark/spark/data/mllib/lr_data.txt 3 10

It gives error messages:
Error in strsplit(part, " ", fixed = T) : non-character argument

It seems that the in "readPartition" function, "part" as a list is fed to "strsplit" directly. An easy fix is to lapply part with strsplit. Does anybody have the issue when running the example before?
